q2: SELECT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM frequents AS f1, frequents AS f2 GROUP BY f1.drinker, f2.drinker HAVING COUNT(f1.times_a_week) = COUNT(f2.times_a_week) AND (f1.drinker <> f2.drinker AND f1.drinker < f2.drinker)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f1, (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f2 WHERE f1.drinker < f2.drinker AND f1.st = f2.st
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM frequents AS f1, frequents AS f2 GROUP BY f1.drinker, f2.drinker HAVING COUNT(f1.times_a_week) = COUNT(f2.times_a_week) AND (f1.drinker <> f2.drinker AND f1.drinker < f2.drinker)
explanation: Q1 compares the sum of times_a_week for each drinker across two aggregated subqueries, returning pairs where sums are equal. Q2 performs a cross join on the Frequents table and groups by drinker pairs, but the HAVING condition COUNT(f1.times_a_week) = COUNT(f2.times_a_week) is always true (due to cross product structure). Thus, Q2 returns all pairs where f1.drinker < f2.drinker, regardless of sum equality. When sums differ, Q1 returns nothing while Q2 returns the pair.
counterexample_dsp: Two drinkers (Alice, Bob) with different total times_a_week. Q1 returns no rows, Q2 returns (Alice, Bob).
